top_story: A month after Tehran warned it would widen the confrontation if Washington struck Iran’s power grid, the Strait of Hormuz has shifted from coercive rhetoric to armed disruption: Iran seized two vessels on 22 April after a ship came under fire, framing the move as retaliation for a US seizure of an Iranian commercial vessel. Hours later, gunfire struck at least three container ships in the same waterway, showing a fast-moving cycle of reprisal that now threatens commercial traffic through one of the region’s most critical chokepoints. This escalation is unfolding against a broader regional landscape already defined by severe civilian harm, including a sharp rise in stillbirths and congenital anomalies in Gaza linked to the sustained effects of war. The immediate takeaway is that intensifying US-Iran confrontation is no longer contained to signaling and is compounding a regional crisis in which economic insecurity and civilian suffering are mutually reinforcing.
